breaches.description: Between 22 and 24 August 2018 Air Canada detected unusual logins to its mobile app, and about 20,000 of 1.7 million profiles may have been accessed. Profiles could include saved passport details. Air Canada locked all app accounts and made every user reset their password.

statement.title: Notice to Air Canada mobile App users

breaches.title: 2024 theft from a cloud database
breaches.affected: About 2.3 million people, mostly job applicants and employees
breaches.description: In 2024 attackers took data from a cloud database used by Advance Auto Parts, a US car parts retailer, part of a wave of attacks on companies’ Snowflake cloud accounts. Files held Social Security and other ID numbers of current and former job applicants and employees.
breaches.source_name: Advance Auto Parts filing (US Securities and Exchange Commission)

breaches.title: Theft of data handled for government and health clients
breaches.description: Conduent processes payments and records for US state governments and health insurers. In January 2025 it found an attacker had been in part of its network and had taken files with personal information of people served by its clients. Filings with US states put the number affected at about 10.5 million.
breaches.source_name: Conduent filing (US Securities and Exchange Commission)

breaches.title: 2024 cyber attack
breaches.affected: About 160,000 people, mostly employees and their families
breaches.description: In late 2024 a cyber attack on Krispy Kreme disrupted online ordering in parts of the US. Personal data was taken, mostly of current and former employees and their families.
breaches.source_name: Krispy Kreme filing (US Securities and Exchange Commission)

breaches.title: Employee leaked staff payroll data
breaches.description: In 2014 a Morrisons employee with a grudge copied payroll data for the UK supermarket’s whole workforce and posted details of nearly 100,000 staff online. He was jailed. Employees sued Morrisons, but in 2020 the UK Supreme Court ruled the company was not responsible for what he did.

outcomes.text: UK Supreme Court ruled Morrisons was not liable for the employee’s leak

breaches.title: 2024 ransomware attack on NHS pathology services
breaches.affected: Patients of London NHS hospitals; Synnovis did not give a total
categories: Blood test results and other pathology data
breaches.description: On 3 June 2024 a ransomware attack hit Synnovis, which runs blood testing for several London NHS hospitals. Operations and blood transfusions were cancelled or delayed for weeks. The attackers later published stolen data, including patient test information.

statement.title: Synnovis’ statement on this week’s cyberattack

breaches.title: 2015–2016 payment card malware
breaches.affected: Cards used at about 1,000 franchised US restaurants
breaches.description: From autumn 2015 attackers used a supplier’s stolen login to put malware on payment systems at Wendy’s franchised restaurants in the US. It first said fewer than 300 restaurants were affected, then found a second type of malware at many more. Wendy’s said its own company-run restaurants were not affected.

statement.title: Payment Card Incident

breaches.title: 2008 card data theft from a payment processor
breaches.affected: Tens of millions of payment cards; no exact total given
breaches.description: In 2008 malware in the network of Heartland, a large US card payment processor, captured card data as it passed through unencrypted. It was announced in January 2009 and was one of the largest card breaches of its time. Heartland paid card companies and cardholders to settle claims, and spent about $148 million on the breach in total.
breaches.source_name: Heartland filing (US Securities and Exchange Commission)

statement.title: Heartland Payment Systems press release (January 2009)

outcomes.text: Settled with American Express ($3.6 million) and later other card companies

breaches.title: Marketing database left open online
breaches.description: A Virgin Media marketing database was set up wrongly and could be accessed from the internet for about ten months until researchers reported it in 2020. It held contact details of about 900,000 people, customers and non-customers. Virgin Media said there were no passwords or financial details, and UK regulators closed the matter without action.

statement.title: Virgin Media’s data incident

breaches.title: Card data theft through a chat supplier
breaches.description: From 26 September to 12 October 2017 malware at [24]7.ai, a chat software supplier, could capture card details that customers typed on Delta’s desktop website. Delta said it couldn’t tell for sure whether anyone’s details were actually taken, offered free credit monitoring and said customers would not pay for any fraud.

statement.title: Information on [24]7.ai cyber incident

breaches.title: 2013–2014 payment card malware
breaches.affected: About 2.6 million cards at Michaels and 400,000 at Aaron Brothers
breaches.description: From May 2013 to January 2014 malware on payment systems at some Michaels and Aaron Brothers craft stores in the US captured card numbers and expiry dates. About 2.6 million Michaels cards and 400,000 Aaron Brothers cards may have been affected. The company said names, addresses and PINs were not at risk.
breaches.source_name: Michaels filing (US Securities and Exchange Commission)

breaches.title: 2017 payment card malware
breaches.affected: Cards used at most Chipotle restaurants during the period; no total given
breaches.description: Between 24 March and 18 April 2017 malware on payment devices at most Chipotle and Pizzeria Locale restaurants captured card details. Chipotle said no other customer information was affected and published a list of locations and dates.

statement.title: Chipotle Mexican Grill Reports Findings from Investigation of Payment Card Security Incident

breaches.title: Two 2014 payment card intrusions
breaches.affected: Cards used at some stores; no total given
breaches.description: In 2014 attackers got into the card payment network of Supervalu, a US grocery company, twice: first between June and July at stores such as Cub Foods, Farm Fresh and Shop ’n Save, and again later that year. Supervalu offered affected customers identity protection.
breaches.source_name: Supervalu filing (US Securities and Exchange Commission)

statement.title: Supervalu announcement of criminal intrusion (August 2014)

breaches.title: 2017 payment card malware
breaches.affected: Cards used at certain drive-ins; no total given
breaches.description: In September 2017 Sonic’s card processor reported suspicious activity on cards used at some Sonic Drive-In restaurants, and malware was found. Sonic offered affected guests two years of free identity theft protection and faced several class actions.
breaches.source_name: Sonic filing (US Securities and Exchange Commission)

breaches.title: 2017 theft of customer email addresses
breaches.affected: DocuSign account holders; no total given
breaches.description: In May 2017 an attacker got into a DocuSign system used for service announcements and took a list of customer email addresses, which were then used for convincing fake DocuSign emails carrying malware. DocuSign said documents, names, passwords and payment data were not affected.

statement.title: Latest update on malicious email campaign (May 2017)

breaches.title: 2014 payment card malware
breaches.affected: About 1.16 million payment cards at 115 US stores
breaches.description: Between August and September 2014 malware on payment systems at 115 of Staples’ more than 1,400 US stores captured card details. About 1.16 million cards may have been affected. Staples offered free identity protection and added new encryption to its tills.

statement.title: Staples Provides Update on Data Security Incident

breaches.title: 2017 card data theft at in-store bars and restaurants
breaches.affected: Cards used at taprooms and table-service restaurants in some stores
breaches.description: Between March and September 2017 malware copied card details at taprooms and full table-service restaurants inside some Whole Foods stores, which used a separate payment system. Cards used at the main checkouts and on Amazon were not affected.

statement.title: Whole Foods Market Payment Card Investigation Update

breaches.title: 2017 payment card malware
breaches.affected: Cards used at some US stores; no total given
categories: Payment card data read from the card
breaches.description: Between April and November 2017 encryption was switched off on some payment devices at Forever 21 stores in the US, and malware on them searched for card data. Cards used on the website were not affected.

statement.title: Forever 21 Reports Findings from Investigation of Payment Card Security Incident

breaches.title: 2014 payment card malware
categories: Payment card data read from the card
breaches.description: In February 2014 malware on payment systems at Sally Beauty, a US beauty supply chain, captured card data from fewer than 25,000 transactions. The company removed the malware. It disclosed a second, separate incident a year later.
breaches.source_name: Sally Beauty filing (US Securities and Exchange Commission)

breaches.title: 2012 theft of card data from a payment processor
breaches.affected: Fewer than 1.5 million card numbers may have been taken
categories: Payment card data read from the card (numbers and expiry dates)
breaches.description: In early 2012 attackers got into part of the processing system of Global Payments, a large US card payment processor, in North America and may have taken card data. The company said fewer than 1.5 million card numbers could have been exported, and that names, addresses and Social Security numbers were not taken. It recorded a pre-tax charge of $84.4 million.
breaches.source_name: Global Payments filing (US Securities and Exchange Commission)

statement.title: Global Payments update on data security incident (April 2012)

breaches.title: 2023 ransomware attack in Australia and New Zealand
breaches.affected: Customers, staff and others in Australia and New Zealand; no total given in the notice
categories: Copies of driver’s licences, passports, Medicare cards and visas (some people)
breaches.description: In December 2023 attackers got into the systems of Nissan’s Australian and New Zealand businesses, including Nissan Financial Services, and later published stolen data on the dark web. For some people this included copies of ID documents and tax file numbers. Nissan offered credit monitoring and paid to replace ID documents.

statement.title: Notice: Cyber security incident impacting Nissan Australia and New Zealand

breaches.title: Customer data left open in the cloud
categories: Data derived from driver’s licence numbers
breaches.description: Two cloud storage containers of Wegmans, a US supermarket chain, were set up so anyone could reach them, one of them since January 2018. They held customer database backups, including email addresses and passwords, until a researcher reported it in April 2021. In 2022 Wegmans paid $400,000 to New York State and agreed to tighten its security.

outcomes.text: Paid $400,000 to New York State

breaches.title: Repeated break-ins to customer accounts
breaches.affected: Tens of thousands of customer accounts
breaches.description: From 2015 attackers used passwords leaked from other sites to break into tens of thousands of Dunkin’ app and website accounts and use the money on stored cards. New York’s Attorney General sued, saying Dunkin’ did not properly investigate or tell customers. In 2020 Dunkin’ agreed to pay $650,000, refund customers and reset passwords.

outcomes.text: Sued by New York’s Attorney General
Paid $650,000 to New York and agreed to refund customers

breaches.title: Two hotel payment card breaches
breaches.description: Attackers put card-stealing malware on 39 systems at five Trump hotels, including Trump SoHo New York, and a second breach followed in 2016. More than 70,000 card numbers were exposed. In 2016 the company paid $50,000 to New York State and agreed to improve its security.

outcomes.text: Paid $50,000 to New York State

breaches.title: Lost unencrypted backup tapes
breaches.description: In 2012 TD Bank lost unencrypted backup tapes in transit in Massachusetts. They held personal information of about 260,000 US customers. In 2014 the bank settled with nine US states and agreed to encrypt backup tapes before moving them.

outcomes.text: Settled with nine US states

breaches.title: 2019–2020 theft of card data at checkout
breaches.description: From July 2019 to July 2020 attackers used a known flaw in the checkout of Filters Fast, a US online seller of water and air filters, to steal card details. The company missed a warning in February 2020 and only told customers in August 2020. It paid New York State in 2021 and agreed to a full security programme.

outcomes.text: Agreed to pay $200,000 to New York State ($100,000 suspended)

breaches.title: Attacks on the online quote tool
breaches.description: From January 2021 scammers used Root’s online car insurance quote tool, which showed full driver’s licence numbers in a PDF, to collect about 73,000 licence numbers, mostly of New Yorkers, for unemployment fraud. In 2025 Root paid $975,000 to New York State.

outcomes.text: Paid $975,000 to New York State

breaches.title: Attacks on the online quote tool
breaches.description: Noblr’s online car insurance quote tool showed full driver’s licence numbers in several places. From January 2021 scammers abused it to collect licence numbers, some used for unemployment fraud during the pandemic. Noblr was slow to notice because it did not watch site traffic in real time. It paid $500,000 to New York State in 2024.

outcomes.text: Paid $500,000 to New York State

breaches.title: Theft of card data from the online store
breaches.description: Attackers took card details from customers of Acer’s online store. Discover found Acer was the last legitimate shop used by hundreds of cards later used for fraud. In 2017 Acer paid $115,000 to New York State and agreed to keep up card industry security standards.

outcomes.text: Paid $115,000 to New York State

breaches.title: Social Security numbers printed on mailing labels
categories: Social Security numbers (printed on mailing labels)
breaches.description: In 2016 EmblemHealth, a New York health insurer, posted Medicare drug plan packets to 81,122 members with each person’s Social Security number printed on the mailing label, as part of their insurance claim number. In 2018 it paid $575,000 to New York State and agreed to check its mailings.

outcomes.text: Paid $575,000 to New York State

breaches.title: 2012 hack of insurance quote data
breaches.description: In October 2012 hackers took data of 1.27 million people from Nationwide, a US insurer, through a flaw it had not patched. Many had only asked for a quote and never became customers, but Nationwide kept their data. In 2017 it paid $5.5 million to 33 US states.

outcomes.text: Paid $5.5 million to 33 US states

breaches.title: 2021 ransomware attack on a college
breaches.description: In November 2021 a hacker got into the systems of Marymount Manhattan College in New York, accessed data of more than 190,000 current, past and prospective students and staff, and demanded a ransom, which the college paid. In 2023 it agreed with New York’s Attorney General to spend $3.5 million on security, including two-step login.

outcomes.text: Agreed to spend $3.5 million on security under a deal with New York’s Attorney General

breaches.title: 2021 ransomware attack on a home care company
breaches.description: In January 2021 an employee of Personal Touch, a Long Island home health care company, opened a malicious attachment in a phishing email, which let ransomware attackers in. Unencrypted patient files of about 316,845 New Yorkers were exposed. In 2023 Personal Touch paid $350,000 to New York State and offered free credit monitoring.

outcomes.text: Paid $350,000 to New York State

breaches.title: 2020 ransomware attack on a medical billing company
breaches.description: In December 2020 ransomware attackers took 79,000 files from Practicefirst, a medical management company in Erie County, New York, that handles billing for doctors. More than 1.2 million people were affected. New York’s Attorney General found it had not updated its software or tested its security, and it paid $550,000 in 2023.

outcomes.text: Paid $550,000 to New York State

breaches.title: 2021 ransomware attack on a health centre
breaches.description: In May 2021 ransomware attackers got into Refuah Health Center, a Hudson Valley health provider, and reached files on more than 260,000 patients. It had not closed old accounts, used two-step login or encrypted patient data. In 2024 it agreed to spend $1.2 million on security and pay New York State.

outcomes.text: Agreed to spend $1.2 million on security and pay $450,000 ($100,000 suspended)

breaches.title: 2023 ransomware attacks on a medical practice
breaches.description: In 2023 ransomware attackers got into the systems of Albany ENT & Allergy, a medical practice in New York’s Capital Region, and reached patient records of 213,935 New Yorkers. It had no in-house security expert and did not properly oversee its IT suppliers. In 2024 it agreed to pay $500,000 and spend $2.25 million on security.

outcomes.text: Paid $500,000 and agreed to spend $2.25 million on security

breaches.title: 2021 phishing attack on a dental insurer
breaches.description: In late 2021 a customer service employee at Healthplex, a New York dental insurance company, clicked a phishing email and gave attackers access to an email account holding consumer health data. It had no two-step login on email and reported the breach months late. New York’s financial regulator fined it $2 million in 2025.
breaches.source_name: New York State Department of Financial Services

outcomes.text: Fined $2 million by New York’s financial regulator

breaches.title: Phishing of employee email accounts
categories: Customer personal information and insurance claims
breaches.description: From September 2018 phishing emails tricked employees of First Unum and Paul Revere, US insurers owned by Unum, into giving away their email passwords. Customer data in those mailboxes was exposed. The companies had not fully set up two-step login, despite certifying they had. New York’s financial regulator fined them $1.8 million in 2021.
breaches.source_name: New York State Department of Financial Services

outcomes.text: Fined $1.8 million by New York’s financial regulator

breaches.title: 2021 ransomware attack on a law firm
breaches.affected: Patients and others named in legal files; no total given in the summary
categories: Medical and personal information in legal files
breaches.description: Around Christmas 2021 LockBit ransomware hit HPMB, a New York law firm that represents hospitals in lawsuits, and the firm paid a $100,000 ransom. Its files held patients’ medical and personal information. The firm later settled with New York’s Attorney General.

outcomes.text: Settled with New York’s Attorney General

breaches.title: Breach of employee data at a cinema company
breaches.affected: More than 23,000 New York employees and contractors
breaches.description: An attacker used an employee’s stolen VPN login, which had no two-step login, to get into the network of National Amusements, which runs Showcase Cinemas. Data of more than 23,000 New York employees and contractors was exposed, and the company waited over a year to tell them. It said cinema customers were not affected. It paid $250,000 to New York State in 2024.

outcomes.text: Paid $250,000 to New York State

breaches.title: 2023 attack through an unpatched flaw
breaches.description: HealthAlliance, which runs hospitals in New York’s Hudson Valley, knew of a security flaw but couldn’t patch it and kept the system running. In September and October 2023 attackers used it to steal patient and employee records. In 2024 it agreed to a $1.4 million penalty, of which it pays $550,000.

outcomes.text: Agreed to a $1.4 million penalty, paying $550,000 (the rest suspended)

breaches.title: Ransomware attack and data breach at an accounting firm
breaches.description: Wojeski & Company, an accounting firm in Albany, New York, suffered a ransomware attack in July 2023 and a data breach in May 2024, exposing clients’ personal and financial details. In 2025 it paid $60,000 to New York State and agreed to tighten its security.

outcomes.text: Paid $60,000 to New York State

breaches.title: 2021 attack through an old network device
breaches.description: In December 2021 an attacker used a known flaw in outdated network hardware to get into US Radiology Specialists and stole personal and health information of 198,260 patients of Windsong Radiology in Western New York. In 2023 it paid $450,000 to New York State.

outcomes.text: Paid $450,000 to New York State

breaches.title: 2023 theft of patient and employee files
breaches.description: In 2023 attackers used a stolen login to get remote access to the network of OrthopedicsNY, an orthopaedic practice in New York’s Capital Region, and downloaded unencrypted files about 656,000 patients and employees. In 2025 it paid $500,000 to New York State and funded a year of free credit monitoring.

outcomes.text: Paid $500,000 to New York State

breaches.title: Theft from a server of card data stored since 2002
breaches.affected: Up to 1.8 million payment cards and 1.2 million logins
breaches.description: An attacker got into the shop server of Sports Warehouse, which runs online stores such as Tennis Warehouse and Running Warehouse. It held payment card details for nearly every purchase since 2002, in plain text, plus customer logins. In 2023 the company paid $300,000 to New York State.

outcomes.text: Paid $300,000 to New York State

breaches.title: 2015 cyber attack
breaches.affected: More than 3 million customers and 1,000 employees
breaches.description: In 2015 attackers got into a computer system of Carphone Warehouse, a UK mobile phone retailer, using old software it had not kept up to date. Personal data of more than 3 million customers and 1,000 employees was exposed, including historical card details for some customers. The UK Information Commissioner’s Office fined the company £400,000 in 2018.
breaches.source_name: UK Information Commissioner’s Office, data security report

outcomes.text: Fined £400,000 by the UK Information Commissioner’s Office

breaches.title: 2011 break-in to the Steam forums and a Steam database
breaches.affected: Steam users; Valve gave no total
breaches.description: In November 2011 attackers defaced the Steam forums and got into a Steam database holding usernames, scrambled (salted and hashed) passwords, purchase history, email and billing addresses and encrypted card details. Valve made forum users reset their passwords. In February 2012 it said the attackers had probably copied a backup of Steam transactions from 2004 to 2008, without Steam passwords, and that it had no evidence card details were misused.

statement.title: Message from Gabe to Steam Community

breaches.title: 2015 Steam Store caching error
categories: Last four digits of Steam Guard phone numbers
Partial payment card numbers (last two digits)
breaches.description: On 25 December 2015, during a cyber attack on Steam, a configuration mistake made the Steam Store show some users’ account pages to other users for about 90 minutes. Pages of about 34,000 users may have been seen. Valve said full card numbers and passwords were not shown and nobody could make changes to other accounts.

statement.title: Update on Christmas Issues
